answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for a database account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create: az cosmosdb create --name <account> --resource-group <rg> --locations regionName=<region> --default-consistency-level Session. This is in the core Azure CLI (no separate extension required for basic create/manage operations).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account. Example Bicep resource: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: accountName ... } . Example Terraform: resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "..." location = "..." offer_type = "Standard" consistency_policy { default_consistency_level = "Session" } }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB-compatible (DocumentDB) endpoint you use a Mongo connection string. Typical form: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. You can also use mongodb+srv:// if the account supports SRV; otherwise use the explicit host + port 10255 and include ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, and retryWrites=false in query options.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB / Mongo-compatible) is billed primarily on Request Units (RUs) for provisioned throughput (manual RU/s or autoscale). There is also a serverless option for some accounts and dedicated vCore-based clusters exist in specific SKUs/offers. In practice start with provisioned RUs (or autoscale) and adjust; serverless is limited and dedicated vCore tiers are separate offerings.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Mongo-compatible API authenticates with Mongo credentials (username/password / SCRAM). Cosmos DB account keys / primary connection strings are used for the control plane; the Mongo driver authenticates with the Mongo user credential provided by the account. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is not generally supported for the Mongo API drivers — AAD integration exists for other Cosmos DB APIs (SQL) but not as a native MongoDB wire-protocol auth method. So drivers should use the Mongo credential in the connection string (SCRAM).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., mongodb Node.js driver) or higher-level ODMs like Mongoose for Node.js. There is no separate Mongo-specific Azure SDK for application data access; treat the service as a MongoDB endpoint and use the official Mongo drivers/ODM.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: From the MongoDB-compatible API surface I would expect vector index support to follow MongoDB 7+ syntax (examples in other Mongo deployments): db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vector: { dims: 1536, similarity: 'cosine', algorithm: 'hnsw' } }). That said, support and exact options (HNSW, IVF, DiskANN etc.) depend on the managed offering and SKU; if vector indexes are available you typically create them with a createIndex call that specifies the field type 'vector' and algorithm options. (I am uncertain about exact option names for this Azure variant.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Options: (1) Use MongoDB text indexes for simple full-text searches (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' })). (2) For richer full-text or hybrid vector+text search, index Cosmos DB content into Azure Cognitive Search and use its full-text + semantic/vector capabilities. On the Mongo API you typically either rely on Mongo text indexes or an external Azure Cognitive Search indexer that reads the collection.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Azure's Mongo-compatible offering exposes specific Mongo server protocol versions (historically 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4 and more recently 5.0/6.0 and newer in managed clusters). Exact supported server-major versions depend on the account configuration; many managed accounts now support 6.x (and some offer 7.0 compatibility). Some MongoDB features are limited or behave differently (server-side JavaScript, certain admin commands, file storage via GridFS edge cases, and some aggregation stages/transaction semantics may be restricted). Always verify the account's supported server version and feature matrix before relying on cutting-edge features.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB emulator for SQL/Table/Gremlin APIs, but for Mongo API development it's common to run a local MongoDB server (official docker image) for functional testing: docker run --name local-mongo -p 27017:27017 -d mongo:7.0. Use port 27017 in your local connection strings. The Cosmos emulator does not fully emulate the Mongo wire-protocol in many cases, so use a real Mongo image locally or test against the live managed cluster when necessary.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams (MongoDB change streams) are available on recent Mongo-compatible versions in managed offerings, but support can depend on the account SKU/version. Alternatively Cosmos DB exposes its own Change Feed (different API). For Mongo change streams you typically need a replica-set-capable account and a server version that advertises change stream support; no special extra toggle beyond using a compatible account, but you should confirm on the specific cluster. (If using the Cosmos Change Feed, that is a separate feature you can query via the Cosmos SDK.)

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (the prompt references a 'documentdb' MCP server). The general Azure MCP server covers generic ARM/control operations, but Mongo-specific data-plane inspection and tooling are provided by the documentdb MCP server/agent set.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's document database service; it later evolved/was rebranded into Azure Cosmos DB (multi-model, global). The 'DocumentDB' name historically referred to that Microsoft service and is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB. The Cosmos DB Mongo-compatible API is an API surface on top of the Cosmos DB engine providing Mongo wire-protocol compatibility.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath the Mongo-compatible endpoint is the Cosmos DB storage/engine (not a stock MongoDB server). The Mongo driver talks the Mongo wire protocol and Cosmos translates calls into its engine semantics. Application code using standard Mongo drivers and basic CRUD/aggregation patterns will mostly work, but there are semantic differences and feature gaps (transactions, certain commands, performance characteristics) you must validate against the managed engine.

answers.question: What database name should this sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_customer_360_01 for everything the sample creates.

answers.question: Which environment variable contains the connection string and how should the app read it?
answers.answer: The connection string is provided in the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI. Read it at runtime (e.g., in Node.js: const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI) and do not hard-code the value in any file or logs.

answers.question: Which Node.js client and connection options should the sample use?
answers.answer: Use Mongoose (backed by the official mongodb driver). Example connection code: const mongoose = require('mongoose'); await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates: false, retryWrites: false, replicaSet: 'globaldb' }); Adjust options to include ssl/tls and replicaSet=globaldb as required by the managed endpoint.

answers.question: What index definition does this sample need for identity resolution?
answers.answer: Create a unique index on customerId to allow fast upserts: db.customers.createIndex({ customerId: 1 }, { unique: true, name: 'idx_unique_customerId' }).

answers.question: What update pattern will the sample use to merge source-specific attributes without overwriting unrelated fields?
answers.answer: Use an upsert with $set targeted to a source-specific sub-document. Example Mongoose-style update: await Customer.updateOne( { customerId }, { $set: { [`sources.${sourceKey}`]: sourcePayload, updatedAt: new Date() }, $setOnInsert: { createdAt: new Date() } }, { upsert: true } ); This updates only the named sources.<sourceKey> subdocument and avoids clobbering other fields.
